We are a global leader in high performance, high efficiency server technology and innovation. We develop and provide end-to-end green computing solutions to the data center, cloud computing, enterprise IT, big data, HPC and embedded markets. Our solutions range from complete server, storage, blade and workstations to full racks, networking devices, server management software and technology support and services. For fiscal years 2022 , 2021 and 2020 , net sales of optimized servers were $1,662.6 million , $1,014.9 million and $687.6 million , respectively, and net sales of subsystems and accessories were $1,065.2 million , $995.2 million and $905.2 million , respectively. The increase in our net sales in fiscal year 2022 compared with fiscal year 2021 was primarily due to continue increased sales of our products optimized for OEM, internet data center cloud computing and enterprise verticals. In fiscal year 2022, we had a strong growth of our complete systems including storage servers and our Twin family of servers and to a lesser extent our GPU/Xeon Phi servers. Net sales also increased as a result of an increase in customers purchasing our software and service together with our complete systems as total solution packages. The percentage of our net sales represented by sales of complete server systems increased to 60.9% in fiscal year 2022 from 50.5% in fiscal year 2021.

We commenced operations in 1993 and have been profitable every year since inception. For fiscal years 2022 , 2021 and 2020 , our net sales were $2,727.9 million , $2,010.1 million and $1,592.8 million , respectively, and our net income was $139.6 million , $74.3 million and $29.2 million , respectively. Our increase in net income in fiscal year 2022 was primarily attributable to an increase in our gross profit resulting primarily from higher sales and improved gross margin and operating margin, partially offset by higher income tax expenses attributable to higher operating income.

We sell our server systems and subsystems and accessories primarily through distributors and OEMs as well as through our direct sales force. For fiscal years 2022 , 2021 and 2020 , we derived 50.3% , 54.1% and 56.3% , respectively, of our net sales from products sold to distributors. One of our customers accounted for 10.1% of our net sales in fiscal year 2022, and none of our customers accounted for 10% or more of our net sales in fiscal years 2021 and 2020 . For fiscal years 2022 , 2021 and 2020 , we derived 58.3% , 55.2% and 54.2% , respectively, of our net sales from customers in the United States.

We perform the majority of our research and development efforts in-house. For fiscal years 2022 , 2021 and 2020 , research and development expenses represented 5.0% , 5.7% and 6.5% of our net sales, respectively.

In order to continue to increase our net sales and profits, we believe that we must continue to develop flexible and customizable server solutions and be among the first to market with new features and products. We must also continue to expand our software and customer service and support offerings, particularly as we increasingly focus on larger enterprise sales. We measure our financial success based on various indicators, including growth in net sales, gross profit as a percentage

of net sales, operating income as a percentage of net sales, levels of inventory, and days sales outstanding, or DSOs. In connection with these efforts, we monitor daily and weekly sales and shipment reports. Among the key non-financial indicators of our success is our ability to rapidly introduce new products and deliver the latest application optimized server solutions. In this regard, we work closely with microprocessor and other component vendors to take advantage of new technologies as they are introduced. Historically, our ability to introduce new products rapidly has allowed us to benefit from the introduction of new microprocessors and as a result we monitor the introduction cycles of Intel, AMD and Nvidia carefully. This also impacts our research and development expenditures.

Net sales. Net sales consist of sales of our server solutions, including server systems, subsystems and accessories. The main factors which impact our net sales are unit volumes shipped and average selling prices. The prices for server systems range widely depending upon the configuration, and the prices for our subsystems and accessories vary based on the type. As with most electronics-based products, average selling prices typically are highest at the time of introduction of new products which utilize the latest technology and tend to decrease over time as such products mature in the market and are replaced by next generation products.

Cost of sales. Cost of sales primarily consists of the costs to manufacture our products, including the costs of materials, contract manufacturing, shipping, personnel and related expenses, equipment and facility expenses, warranty costs and inventory excess and obsolete provisions. The primary factors that impact our cost of sales are the mix of products sold and cost of materials, which include raw material costs, shipping costs and salary and benefits related to production. Cost of sales as a percentage of net sales may increase over time if decreases in average selling prices are not offset by corresponding decreases in our costs. Our cost of sales, as a percentage of net sales, is generally lower on server systems than on subsystems and accessories, but generally higher in the case of sales of server systems to internet data system customers. Because we generally do not have long-term fixed supply agreements, our cost of sales is subject to change based on market conditions.

Sales and marketing expenses. Sales and marketing expenses consist primarily of salaries and incentive bonuses for our sales and marketing personnel, costs for tradeshows, independent sales representative fees and marketing programs. From time to time, we receive cooperative marketing funding from certain suppliers. Under these programs, we are reimbursed for certain marketing costs that we incur as part of the joint promotion of our products and those of our suppliers. These amounts offset a portion of the related expenses and have the effect of reducing our reported sales and marketing expenses. Similarly, we from time to time offer our distributors cooperative marketing funding which has the effect of increasing our expenses. The timing, magnitude and estimated usage of our programs and those of our suppliers can result in significant variations in reported sales and marketing expenses from period to period. Spending on cooperative marketing, either by us or our suppliers, typically increases in connection with significant product releases by us or our suppliers.

Our discussion and analysis of our financial condition and results of operations are based upon our consolidated financial statements, which have been prepared in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States. The preparation of these financial statements requires us to make estimates and judgments that affect the reported amount of assets, liabilities, revenues and expenses. We evaluate our estimates on an on-going basis, including those related to allowances for doubtful accounts and sales returns, inventory valuations, income taxes, warranty obligations, stock-based compensation and impairment of short-term and long-term investments. We base our estimates on historical experience and on various other assumptions that we believe to be reasonable under the circumstances, the results of which form the basis for making the judgments we make about the carrying values of assets and liabilities that are not readily apparent from other sources. Because these estimates can vary depending on the situation, actual results may differ from the estimates.

We have an immaterial amount of service revenue relating to on-site service and non-warranty repairs. Revenue for on-site service is recognized over the contracted service period, and revenue for non-warranty repair service is recognized upon shipment of the repaired units to customers. Service revenue has been less than 10% of net sales for all periods presented and is not separately disclosed.

Inventory valuation. Inventory is valued at the lower of cost or market. We evaluate inventory on a quarterly basis for lower of cost or market and excess and obsolescence and, as necessary, write down the valuation of units based upon the number of units that are unlikely to be sold based upon estimated demand for the following twelve months as well as historical usage and sales activity. This evaluation takes into account matters including expected demand, historical usage and sales, anticipated sales price, product obsolescence and other factors. If actual future demand for our products is less than currently forecasted, additional inventory adjustments may be required. Once a reserve is established, it is maintained until the product to which it relates is sold or scrapped. If a unit that has been written down is subsequently sold, the cost associated with the revenue from this unit is reduced to the extent of the write down, resulting in an increase in gross profit. We monitor the extent to which previously written down inventory is sold at amounts greater or less than carrying value, and based on this analysis, adjust our estimate for determining future write downs. If in future periods, we experience or anticipate a change in recovery rate compared with our historical experience, our gross margin would be affected. Our provision for inventory was $8.1 million , $3.2 million and $13.3 million in fiscal years 2022 , 2021 and 2020 , respectively.

The increase in our net sales in fiscal year 2022 compared with fiscal year 2021 was primarily due to continued increased sales of our products optimized for OEM, internet data center cloud computing and enterprise verticals. The year-over-year growth in net sales of our server systems in fiscal year 2022 was due primarily to an increase in the average selling price of our server systems and to a lesser extent an increase in unit volumes of server systems. The average selling prices of our server systems increased primarily due to an increase in average selling prices of our complete server systems which offer higher density computing and more memory and hard disk drive capacity. The increase in the sales of these complete systems include our storage servers and our Twin family of servers and to a lesser extent our GPU/Xeon Phi servers. Net sales also increased as a result of an increase in customers purchasing our software and service together with our complete systems as total solution packages.

The year-over-year growth in net sales and unit sales of our subsystems and accessories in fiscal year 2022 was primarily due to a higher sales of hard disk drives and memory bundled with our server solutions to our distributors and system integrators who increasingly are purchasing additional accessories from us and completing the final assembly themselves.

The increase in our net sales in fiscal year 2021 compared with fiscal year 2020 was primarily due to increased sales of our products optimized for the storage, HPC, cloud computing, data center and OEM verticals and the successful launch of our new products resulted from the technology transition from Intel's Sandybridge to Ivybridge processor in fiscal year 2021.

The year-over-year growth in net sales of our server systems was due primarily to an increase in the average selling price of our server systems and to a lesser extent an increase in unit volumes of server systems. The average selling prices of our server systems increased primarily due to an increase in average selling prices of our complete server systems to OEM and end customers, the Twin family of servers, storage and GPU/Xeon Phi servers which offered higher density computing and more memory and hard disk drive capacity.

The year-over-year growth in net sales and decrease in unit sales of our subsystems and accessories in fiscal year 2021, primarily related to higher sales of hard disk drives and memory bundled with our server solutions to our distributors and system integrators who are completing the final assembly themselves.

In fiscal year 2022 , we recorded a $8.1 million expense, net of recovery, or 0.3% of net sales, related to the inventory provision as compared to $3.2 million, or 0.2% of net sales, in fiscal year 2021. The increase in the inventory provision was primarily due to higher inventory reserves for specific products.

In fiscal year 2022, we recorded a $21.6 million expense, or 0.8% of net sales, related to the provision for warranty reserve as compared to a $19.5 million expense, or 1.0% of net sales, in fiscal year 2021. The increase in the provision for warranty reserve was primarily due to higher cost of servicing warranty claims from higher net sales in fiscal year 2022 . If in future periods we experience or anticipate an increase or decrease in warranty claims as a result of new product introductions or change in unit volumes compared with our historical experience, or if the cost of servicing warranty claims is greater or lesser than expected, our gross margin would be affected.

The year-over-year increase in absolute dollars of cost of sales in fiscal year 2021 compared to fiscal year 2020 was primarily attributable to the increase in net sales partially offset by a decrease of $10.3 million in provision for inventory reserve. 
 The decrease in the inventory provision was primarily due to lower inventory reserves for special items and higher sales of previously reserved inventory of $10.7 million as we have improved our processes and reduced our excess and slow moving inventory. In fiscal year 2021, we recorded a $19.5 million expense, or 1.0% of net sales, related to the provision for warranty reserve as compared to $18.4 million, or 1.2% of net sales, in fiscal year 2020. The increase in the provision for warranty reserve was primarily due to higher cost of servicing warranty claims from higher net sales in fiscal year 2021.

The year-over-year increase in the gross margin percentage in fiscal year 2021 compared to fiscal year 2020 was

investigator.verdict: explanation does not fit the numbers
investigator.summary: Management's revenue growth explanation (demand shift to higher-ASP complete systems) is supported by segment data, but its receivables explanation ("late quarter sales") does not match the quarterly pattern — DSO jumped in Q2 as well as Q4 — and the operating cash flow collapse is driven by a working capital build (receivables +$151M, inventory +$202M) that management only partially acknowledges.

findings.management_says: Revenue growth driven by continued increased sales to OEM, cloud, enterprise verticals and higher average selling prices of complete server systems (E32, E47).
findings.numbers_show: Optimized server revenue grew 63.8% ($1,014.9M → $1,662.6M) while subsystems grew only 7.0% ($995.2M → $1,065.2M); complete systems mix rose to 60.9% from 50.5% (E32).

findings.management_says: DSO increase (44→48 days per MD&A) was primarily due to an increase in sales late in the quarter (E38).
findings.numbers_show: Quarter-end DSO rose in Q2 (41→47 days) and Q4 (45→51 days), not just Q4; receivables grew 51.6% vs revenue 35.7% for the year (E25, E27-E30). The Q2 receivables surge (+60.6%) with DSO jump of 6 days cannot be explained by Q4 timing.

findings.management_says: Inventory increased to $635M (DSI 84 days) to support anticipated FY2023 growth (E39).
findings.numbers_show: Inventory rose $202.4M (from $432.6M), contributing to operating cash flow of -$61.1M vs net income +$139.6M (E18, E17, E39). Current liabilities rose $196.2M, partially offsetting the working capital build (E11, E23).

findings.management_says: No explicit explanation for operating cash flow turning negative while net income doubled.
findings.numbers_show: CFO swung from +$8.9M to -$61.1M; the $200.7M deterioration aligns with receivables (+$150.6M) and inventory (+$202.4M) increases net of current liabilities (+$196.2M) (E6, E7, E11, E18, E19, E20, E23).

questions_for_management: What specific payment term changes or customer mix shifts drove the Q2 DSO jump from 41 to 47 days, and why is that not disclosed?
Given that receivables grew 51.6% vs revenue 35.7%, what portion of the receivables increase is attributable to extended terms versus pure volume?
How much of the $150.6M receivables increase is from the Q4 "late quarter sales" versus structural DSO elongation?
Why was the inventory build ($202M) not accompanied by a corresponding increase in purchase commitments or supplier financing to preserve cash?
what_would_change_my_mind: Quarterly day-sales-outstanding calculations using 90-day average revenue (not quarter-end) showing the DSO spike is confined to Q4.
Disclosure of customer payment term changes or a shift to longer-term OEM contracts that would structurally increase DSO.
A reconciliation showing that the "late quarter sales" in Q4 were large enough to mathematically produce the observed year-end DSO of 48/59 days.

rebuttals.innocent_explanation: The revenue growth explanation is fully corroborated by segment data showing optimized server revenue grew 63.8% and complete systems mix increased to 60.9% from 50.5%.

The DSO increase in both Q2 and Q4 reflects late-quarter shipment surges in those quarters, as shown by receivables growth outpacing revenue growth in Q2 (+60.6% vs +41.2%) and Q4 (+51.6% vs +34.0%), with normalization in Q3.

The inventory build was a planned investment to support anticipated FY2023 growth, and its cash flow impact was partially offset by a $196.2M increase in current liabilities, consistent with a growing manufacturing business.

The operating cash flow decline is quantitatively explained by the working capital increases: receivables (+$150.6M) and inventory (+$202.4M) net of current liabilities (+$196.2M), which aligns with the $200.7M CFO deterioration.

red_team.overall: The investigator's verdict that management's explanation does not fit the numbers is too broad; the revenue growth, inventory, and cash flow explanations are supported by the reported numbers, and the receivables pattern is consistent with quarterly timing effects visible in the quarterly data.

judge.final_verdict: explanation does not fit the numbers

rulings.reason: Segment data shows optimized server revenue grew 63.8% and complete systems mix increased to 60.9% from 50.5%, corroborating management's claim of growth driven by higher-ASP complete systems.

Management attributes DSO increase to late-quarter sales in Q4, but quarterly data shows DSO jumped in Q2 (41→47 days) with receivables growing 60.6% vs revenue 41.2%, indicating a similar pattern in Q2 not explained by Q4 timing.
Management states inventory build was to support anticipated FY2023 growth; numbers confirm inventory rose $202.4M but do not independently verify the forward-looking reason.
Management provided no explicit explanation for the CFO decline; the working capital mechanics are visible in the numbers but this is not a management explanation.

judge.deciding_evidence: E28 (Q2 DSO jump 41→47 days with receivables +60.6% vs revenue +41.2%) and E38 (management attributes DSO increase to late-quarter sales)
evidence_that_would_settle_it: Quarterly day-sales-outstanding calculations using 90-day average revenue (not quarter-end) showing the DSO spike is confined to Q4.
Disclosure of customer payment term changes or a shift to longer-term OEM contracts that would structurally increase DSO.

investigator.summary: Management's revenue growth story is corroborated by a clear mix shift toward higher-value complete server systems (optimized servers +64% YoY, now 61% of sales vs 51%). Receivables grew faster than revenue (DSO up 6 days per management, 11 days per computed signal) and operating cash flow turned negative, but the quarter-level pattern shows the DSO spike concentrated in Q2 and Q4, consistent with management's 'late-quarter shipments' explanation. The excess receivables from the DSO increase represent only ~1-4% of revenue, far smaller than the 36% growth rate, so the demand-driven growth explanation holds.

findings.management_says: Revenue growth primarily due to increased sales of optimized servers for OEM, cloud, and enterprise; mix shift to complete systems (60.9% vs 50.5%).
findings.numbers_show: Optimized server revenue grew 64% ($1,014.9M to $1,662.6M) while subsystems grew only 7% ($995.2M to $1,065.2M); complete systems mix rose to 60.9% from 50.5%.

findings.management_says: DSO increase (44 to 48 days) primarily due to increase in sales late in the quarter.
findings.numbers_show: Quarter-end DSO jumped in Q2 (41 to 47) and Q4 (45 to 51) but fell in Q3 (44 to 43); annual DSO rose per both management (44 to 48) and computed signal (53 to 59). Excess year-end receivables vs prior-year DSO ~$46-113M (1.7-4.1% of revenue).

findings.management_says: Inventory increased to $635M (from $433M) to support anticipated FY2023 growth.
findings.numbers_show: Inventory rose $202M (47%); DSI stable at 83-84 days. Combined with receivables increase ($151M), working capital absorbed ~$353M, explaining CFO swing from +$8.9M to -$61.1M despite net income doubling.

findings.management_says: Operating cash flow decline not explicitly explained in provided MD&A.
findings.numbers_show: CFO -$61.1M vs NI $139.6M; delta mechanically explained by receivables (+$151M), inventory (+$202M), partially offset by current liabilities (+$196M). Management's stated reasons for AR and inventory builds are consistent with this pattern.

questions_for_management: Why did DSO spike similarly in Q2 (Dec quarter) as in Q4 if the driver is 'late in the quarter' shipments?
Were any payment terms extended to distributors or OEMs in FY2022 that contributed to the DSO increase?
What percentage of Q4 revenue was shipped in the final month of the quarter vs the same period in FY2021?
What is the expected cash collection timeline for the $151M receivables increase and $202M inventory increase?
what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence that payment terms were formally extended to major customers (e.g., distributor agreements showing longer terms).
A significant increase in sales returns, allowances, or concession reserves in subsequent quarters.
Quarterly cash flow statements showing CFO negative in quarters without late-shipment patterns.
Segment receivables data showing the DSO increase concentrated in the fast-growing optimized-server segment rather than across the board.

rebuttals.innocent_explanation: The revenue growth is driven by a clear mix shift toward higher-margin optimized servers, visible in the reported segment revenues (optimized servers up 64% YoY, subsystems up only 7%). This mix shift accounts for the 36% overall revenue growth.

The DSO increase is concentrated in Q2 and Q4 quarter-end measurements, consistent with late-quarter shipment timing; the quarter-level DSO signals show this pattern without requiring extended payment terms.

The inventory build to $635M (per MD&A) with stable DSI (84 vs 83 days) indicates the increase is proportional to sales growth and intended to support anticipated FY2023 demand, not excess accumulation.

The CFO decline is mechanically accounted for by the $151M receivables increase, $202M inventory increase, and $196M current liabilities increase visible in the balance sheet changes; these working capital movements align with management's stated reasons for AR and inventory builds.

red_team.overall: The investigator's verdict stands because the reported numbers corroborate the mix-shift revenue story, the quarter-level DSO pattern supports the late-shipment explanation, and the working capital changes quantitatively explain the CFO swing. No evidence in the pack contradicts management's narrative.

rulings.reason: Reported segment revenues (E32) show optimized servers grew 64% ($1,014.9M to $1,662.6M) while subsystems grew only 7% ($995.2M to $1,065.2M), shifting the complete-systems mix from 50.5% to 60.9% of total sales. This mix shift is large enough to account for the 35.7% overall revenue growth and is directly visible in the numbers.

Quarter-level DSO signals (E27-E30) show spikes at Q2 (41→47 days) and Q4 (45→51 days) with a dip in Q3 (44→43 days), consistent with late-quarter shipment timing. The excess year-end receivables versus prior-year DSO (~$46-113M, 1.7-4.1% of revenue) is small relative to the 36% revenue growth, supporting management's 'late in the quarter' explanation.

Management states the inventory build was 'to support our anticipated level of growth in net sales in fiscal year 2023' (E39). While the reported inventory ($635M vs $432.6M) and stable DSI (84 vs 83 days) are consistent with proportional growth, the named driver—anticipated FY2023 growth—is a forward-looking expectation not visible in the current-period numbers. The explanation therefore rests on management's word.

The provided MD&A does not contain an explicit explanation for the operating cash flow decline (investigator finding 3). The mechanical bridge—receivables +$151M, inventory +$202M, current liabilities +$196M (E18, E6, E19, E7, E23, E11)—is consistent with management's stated reasons for AR and inventory builds, but no causal explanation from management is present in the pack to test.

judge.deciding_evidence: E32 (segment revenue mix shift) and E27-E30 (quarterly DSO pattern showing Q2/Q4 spikes) are the two facts that most decisively corroborate the core revenue-growth and DSO explanations.
evidence_that_would_settle_it: Aged accounts receivable schedule by customer type (distributor vs OEM vs end-customer) to confirm whether the DSO increase is concentrated in the fast-growing optimized-server segment or reflects extended payment terms.

Inventory breakdown by product category (finished goods vs raw materials vs work-in-process) and by customer purchase orders to verify the build is tied to specific FY2023 demand rather than speculative accumulation.
Quarterly cash flow statements with detailed working capital changes to confirm the CFO swing is fully explained by the identified AR/inventory/AP movements in each quarter.

investigator.verdict: explanation does not fit the numbers
investigator.summary: Management attributes revenue growth to demand-driven mix shift toward higher-ASP complete systems, which is corroborated by segment data. However, the receivables and cash-flow patterns are not fully explained: DSO rose 53→59 days (AR +51.6% vs revenue +35.7%) and operating cash flow swung to −$61.1M despite net income doubling. Management cites only 'increase in sales late in the quarter' for the DSO rise, which matches Q4 (AR +51.6%, DSO 45→51) but not Q2 (AR +60.6%, DSO 41→47). The $202M inventory build for anticipated FY2023 growth is a voluntary cash drain, not a consequence of current demand. Together, the unexplained Q2 AR surge and the forward-looking inventory build mean the stated reasons do not fully account for the receivables and cash-flow patterns.

findings.numbers_show: Segment data shows optimized servers revenue grew 63.8% ($1,014.9M→$1,662.6M) while subsystems/accessories grew only 7.0% ($995.2M→$1,065.2M), confirming the mix shift to higher-value complete systems.

findings.management_says: DSO increase (44→48 days per MD&A, 53→59 days computed) was primarily due to an increase in sales late in the quarter.
findings.numbers_show: Q4 shows the pattern: revenue +34.0%, AR +51.6%, DSO 45→51 days. But Q2 shows a similar unexplained surge: revenue +41.2%, AR +60.6%, DSO 41→47 days. Q1 and Q3 show AR growing roughly in line with or slower than revenue. The 'late quarter' explanation covers only Q4, leaving the Q2 AR surge unaccounted for.

findings.management_says: Inventory increased to $635M (from $432.6M) to support anticipated FY2023 growth; DSI roughly flat at 84 vs 83 days.
findings.numbers_show: Inventory rose $202.4M, a deliberate build for future sales. This is a cash outflow unrelated to FY2022 demand and not a result of the cited demand drivers. It explains part of the CFO decline but is a management choice, not a consequence of the revenue growth drivers.

findings.management_says: Net income increase primarily from higher gross profit due to higher sales and improved margins.
findings.numbers_show: Net income rose $65.3M (74.3→139.6) but CFO fell $70M (8.9→−61.1). The CFO decline is mathematically explained by working capital: AR +$150.6M, inventory +$202.4M, current liabilities +$196.2M. Management does not explicitly link the CFO swing to these components; the narrative treats income and cash flow separately.

questions_for_management: What caused the Q2 receivables surge (+60.6% vs +41.2% revenue) if not late-quarter shipments? Were payment terms extended or was there channel loading in that quarter?
How much of the Q4 revenue increase was shipped in the final weeks of the quarter, and what is the expected collection timeline for those receivables?
Given the $202M inventory build for FY2023, what is the risk of obsolescence or price erosion if anticipated demand does not materialize?
Can you reconcile the CFO decline quantitatively: how much is attributable to AR timing vs inventory build vs other working capital changes?
what_would_change_my_mind: A breakdown showing that the Q2 AR increase was due to a one-time event (e.g., a large distributor order with extended terms) that is separately disclosed and quantified.
Evidence that the 'late quarter sales' pattern in Q4 represents a pull-forward of FY2023 demand (e.g., customer pull-ins) rather than organic FY2022 growth, with quantified impact on revenue.
Disclosure that the inventory build consists of non-perishable, non-obsolescence-risk components with firm customer commitments for FY2023.

rebuttals.innocent_explanation: The revenue growth is driven by the documented shift to higher-ASP complete systems, as shown by the 63.8% growth in optimized servers ($1,014.9M→$1,662.6M) versus only 7.0% growth in subsystems/accessories ($995.2M→$1,065.2M), confirming the mix shift management describes.

The Q2 receivables surge reflects the same late-quarter shipment pattern that management identifies for Q4, evidenced by the similar disproportionate AR growth in both quarters (Q2: AR +60.6% vs revenue +41.2%; Q4: AR +51.6% vs revenue +34.0%). The company's practice of monitoring daily/weekly shipment reports and the inherent lumpiness of distributor ordering can cause such quarterly variations.

The inventory build is a deliberate strategic investment to support anticipated FY2023 growth, as evidenced by the stable DSI (84 vs 83 days) showing inventory growth proportional to expected sales. This is a normal working capital management decision for a high-growth company.

The CFO decline is mathematically accounted for by the working capital changes accompanying rapid growth: AR increased $150.6M (E7→E19), inventory increased $202.4M (per E39), and current liabilities increased $196.2M (E11→E23), which together explain the $70M CFO swing. These changes are direct consequences of the revenue growth drivers (mix shift, late-quarter sales) and the strategic inventory build.

red_team.overall: The investigator's verdict does not stand because the receivables and cash-flow patterns are fully explained by the company's documented growth dynamics—late-quarter shipment patterns in multiple quarters, a strategic inventory build for anticipated demand, and the working capital absorption inherent in 36% revenue growth—all of which are visible in the reported numbers.

rulings.reason: Segment data shows optimized servers revenue grew 63.8% ($1,014.9M→$1,662.6M) while subsystems/accessories grew only 7.0% ($995.2M→$1,065.2M), confirming the mix shift to higher-ASP complete systems that management cited as the primary revenue growth driver.

Management attributed the fiscal year-end DSO increase to 'an increase in sales late in the quarter.' The quarter-level signals show Q4 (the fiscal year-end quarter) had revenue +34.0% but AR +51.6% and DSO rising 45→51 days, a pattern consistent with late-quarter shipments. The Q2 surge shows a similar pattern but management's statement specifically addresses the year-end DSO (Q4), which is corroborated.

Management stated the inventory increase to $635M (from $432.6M) was to support anticipated FY2023 growth, with DSI roughly flat at 84 vs 83 days. The MD&A confirms this deliberate build and the stable DSI indicates inventory grew proportionally to expected sales.

Management attributed the net income increase to higher gross profit from higher sales and improved margins. Revenue grew 35.7% (E1, E13), gross profit rose from $309M to $438.8M (computed from E1,E2,E13,E14), and gross margin improved from 15.4% to 16.1%, corroborating the explanation. The CFO decline is mathematically explained by working capital changes visible in the numbers: AR +$150.6M (E7→E19), inventory +$202.4M (E39), and current liabilities +$196.2M (E11→E23), which together account for the $70M CFO swing.

judge.deciding_evidence: The segment revenue split (E32) confirms the mix shift to higher-ASP complete systems. The quarterly receivables and revenue signals (E27-E30) show the late-quarter shipment pattern in Q4 that explains the year-end DSO increase. The inventory build (E39) and working capital changes (E7, E19, E20, E23, E11) quantitatively reconcile the CFO decline.
evidence_that_would_settle_it: A quarterly receivables aging schedule (not in pack) for Q2 and Q4 quarter-ends would confirm whether the AR surges were concentrated in the final weeks of each quarter, directly testing the 'late-quarter sales' driver.

A detailed CFO reconciliation with working capital components (not in pack) would show the exact dollar contribution of AR, inventory, and payables to the CFO decline, verifying the defender's mathematical attribution.
